# The Gamer's Brain — Celia Hodent (game UX from cognitive science)

- Type: LINK ONLY card (book © the author/publisher; talks free to view via GDC Vault/YouTube).
- Source: Celia Hodent, *The Gamer's Brain: How Neuroscience and UX Can Impact Video Game Design* (CRC Press, 2017; 2nd edition 2025). Compact secondary summary of the framework: https://fjinn.github.io/Experiences/Design/UserExperience/NeuroscienceAndUX.html
- Author: Celia Hodent — psychologist/cognitive scientist; UX director on Fortnite (Epic), previously Ubisoft/LucasArts. The most cited practitioner framework for game UX.

## The reasoning method, distilled

Game UX has two pillars: **usability** (can the player operate it without friction?) and **engage-ability** (does it hold motivation?). Both are constrained by how brains actually work, in three systems:

- **Perception.** Players perceive what they expect to perceive; Gestalt grouping decides what reads as "one thing"; *form follows function* — an element that doesn't look interactive won't be used, and one that does will be clicked even if it isn't. Icons and layouts are read before any text is.
- **Memory.** Working memory is tiny and the forgetting curve is steep. Therefore: don't make the player remember off-screen state or rules taught once, long ago; teach in context, at the moment of need, and restate critical information where it is used.
- **Attention.** Attention is a narrow spotlight, and *inattentional blindness* is real: a player focused on the action will literally not see a quiet change elsewhere on screen, however "obvious" it looks to the designer. Manage workload — minimum necessary information, delivered with enough salience (and context/meaning) to land.

The practical stance: most "players are stupid" bugs are perception/memory/attention bugs in the design.

## For みゅけ

The strip competes for attention with the user's actual desktop work — inattentional blindness is our default condition, not an edge case. State changes that matter (release done, bottleneck, update ready) must earn attention honestly: motion, position at the work cluster, and a redundant channel. See `checklist-brain-and-access.md`.
